explanations.explanation: That's the job, friend. The LORD tells Jeremiah, "Write in a book all the words that I have spoken to you." (Jeremiah 30:2) Not some of them, not the highlights, ALL of them. Jeremiah, the prophet who spoke for the LORD, gets a big writing assignment.

I can see why you'd go there, but the LORD says nothing about the temple here. He tells Jeremiah, "Write in a book all the words that I have spoken to you." (Jeremiah 30:2) The job is writing, and it covers every word He has spoken. Jeremiah's hand is going to be tired.

Nope, these words are not for a locked drawer. I would know, I've been in one. The LORD says, "Write in a book all the words that I have spoken to you." (Jeremiah 30:2) You don't write something in a book to hide it, friend. A book is made to be read.

Yes, friend! The LORD says, "I will restore from captivity My people Israel and Judah." (Jeremiah 30:3) Captivity is not where their story ends. When He says the days are coming, He's talking about a way home.

Whoa, that's the opposite direction. The LORD says the days are coming when He will "restore from captivity My people Israel and Judah." (Jeremiah 30:3) He's pulling them back, not pushing them farther out. Keep your eyes on the way home.

explanations.answer: Leave them in Babylon for good
explanations.explanation: I get why it feels that way, since Babylon looked like a very long stay. But the LORD says, "I will restore from captivity My people Israel and Judah." (Jeremiah 30:3) "For good" is not in His plan. Restoring means bringing them out.

That's it, baker! The LORD says He will restore them to the land He gave their fathers, "and they will possess it." (Jeremiah 30:3) Possess means it's theirs again. They're not just stopping by to look around.

A visit is a nice little trip, friend, but that's not the promise. The LORD says the land is the one He gave their fathers, "and they will possess it." (Jeremiah 30:3) Visiting means you leave again. Possessing means you stay and it's yours.

Oh no, we don't want that word anywhere near this verse. The LORD says He will restore them to the land He gave their fathers, "and they will possess it." (Jeremiah 30:3) The whole verse is about getting back what was gone. Losing is exactly what He's turning around.
Pale, friend! The LORD says He sees "every face turned pale." (Jeremiah 30:6) Picture everyone's color just draining out at once. That's what real terror looks like.

Red is what happens when you're embarrassed or mad, and that's not the picture here. The LORD says He sees "every face turned pale." (Jeremiah 30:6) In this kind of terror the color runs out of the face instead of rushing in. Think of a baker who just heard the oven timer and remembered nothing is in there.

Turning away is a fair guess, since people do that when they're scared. But the LORD says what He sees is "every face turned pale." (Jeremiah 30:6) It's about the color of the face, not the direction it points. The fear is written right there on them.

I see why you'd say that, because the LORD does call it awful. But He says, "None will be like it! It is the time of Jacob's distress, but he will be saved out of it." (Jeremiah 30:7) The distress is real, and so is the rescue. Jacob does not get finished off.
Right, friend! The LORD says, "It is the time of Jacob's distress, but he will be saved out of it." (Jeremiah 30:7) Notice the "but." The day is awful, and Jacob still comes out the other side.

explanations.answer: No more strangers will enslave them
explanations.explanation: That's the promise, friend. The LORD says, "I will break the yoke off their necks and tear off their bonds, and no longer will strangers enslave them." (Jeremiah 30:8) Look at what comes right after. They go from being enslaved to serving the LORD their God (Jeremiah 30:9).

explanations.answer: They will never have to work again
explanations.explanation: Sounds nice, doesn't it? But the LORD never says that. He says, "no longer will strangers enslave them." (Jeremiah 30:8) Being free of strangers is not the same as having nothing to do. In the very next verse they serve the LORD their God (Jeremiah 30:9).

explanations.answer: They will rule over all the nations
explanations.explanation: That's a big jump, friend, and the verse doesn't make it. The LORD says He will break the yoke and tear off the bonds, "and no longer will strangers enslave them." (Jeremiah 30:8) The promise is freedom from the ones who held them. Nothing here says they take over the world.

explanations.answer: The LORD their God and their king
explanations.explanation: Yes! The LORD says, "they will serve the LORD their God and David their king, whom I will raise up for them." (Jeremiah 30:9) They stop serving strangers and start serving the One who is actually theirs. That's a trade I'd make any day.

That's the old arrangement, friend, and it's the one the LORD is ending. He says "no longer will strangers enslave them. Instead, they will serve the LORD their God and David their king." (Jeremiah 30:8-9) The word "instead" does all the work. The yoke comes off.

Not these, baker. The LORD says, "Instead, they will serve the LORD their God and David their king, whom I will raise up for them." (Jeremiah 30:9) Their service goes to the LORD their God and the king He raises up. The gods of the nations don't get a spot on the list.

True, friend! The LORD says, "As for you, O Jacob My servant, do not be afraid... For I will surely save you out of a distant place." (Jeremiah 30:10) He calls Jacob His servant right in the middle of the fear. That's a good way to be talked to.

I think the "distant place" threw you off, but it's actually the good part. The LORD says, "As for you, O Jacob My servant, do not be afraid, declares the LORD... For I will surely save you out of a distant place." (Jeremiah 30:10) He names Jacob as His servant and promises to save him from far away. So this one is true.

That's right, baker! The LORD says, "Jacob will return to quiet and ease, with no one to make him afraid." (Jeremiah 30:10) Quiet, ease and nobody making him afraid. That sounds like a kitchen after the last batch is out and the dishes are done.

After captivity, hard labor sounds like more of the same, doesn't it? But the LORD says, "Jacob will return to quiet and ease, with no one to make him afraid." (Jeremiah 30:10) The way home leads to rest. The heavy work is behind him.

That's a rough picture, friend, and it's not the one the LORD paints. He says, "Jacob will return to quiet and ease, with no one to make him afraid." (Jeremiah 30:10) No one to make him afraid is the opposite of endless war. He comes home to peace.

explanations.answer: He will not completely destroy them
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The LORD says, "Though I will completely destroy all the nations to which I have scattered you, I will not completely destroy you." (Jeremiah 30:11) He's with them to save them, and He says so right there. Their story keeps going.

I can see why that line sounds scary, but listen to the second half. The LORD says, "Though I will completely destroy all the nations to which I have scattered you, I will not completely destroy you." (Jeremiah 30:11) That "not" matters a lot. Right before it He says, "I am with you to save you."

explanations.answer: He will leave them among the nations
explanations.explanation: That's not what He says, baker. He says, "Though I will completely destroy all the nations to which I have scattered you, I will not completely destroy you." (Jeremiah 30:11) The promise is about them not being destroyed. It's a promise to save them, which doesn't fit with leaving them where they are.

I get why you'd think saving means skipping the consequences, but the verse says otherwise. The LORD says, "Yet I will discipline you justly, and will by no means leave you unpunished." (Jeremiah 30:11) Salvation and discipline show up in the same breath. So this one is false.

That's right, friend. The LORD says, "I am with you to save you," and then adds, "Yet I will discipline you justly, and will by no means leave you unpunished." (Jeremiah 30:11) Both are true at once. He saves them, and He doesn't let it go unpunished.

That's it. The LORD says, "All your lovers have forgotten you; they no longer seek you." (Jeremiah 30:14) Nobody pleads their cause, and the ones they counted on aren't even looking for them. Friend, that's a lonely spot.

explanations.answer: They have come to rescue them
explanations.explanation: I wish that were the case, baker, but it's the other way around. The LORD says, "All your lovers have forgotten you; they no longer seek you." (Jeremiah 30:14) No rescue party shows up. They don't even look for them.

explanations.answer: They have paid to free them
explanations.explanation: Nobody's reaching for their wallet here. The LORD says, "All your lovers have forgotten you; they no longer seek you." (Jeremiah 30:14) If they've forgotten them, there's no one left to pay a thing. The verse before says there's no one to plead their cause (Jeremiah 30:13).

True, friend, and it's a heavy one. The LORD says, "I have struck you as an enemy would, with the discipline of someone cruel, because of your great iniquity and your numerous sins." (Jeremiah 30:14) He gives the reason right in the verse. This part is hard, so I'll just say it plainly and let it sit.

I think it's a hard line to accept, so I understand the hesitation. But the LORD does say it: "I have struck you as an enemy would, with the discipline of someone cruel, because of your great iniquity and your numerous sins." (Jeremiah 30:14) The words are right there in the verse. So this one is true.

explanations.answer: The same thing happens to them
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker! The LORD says, "all who devour you will be devoured... Those who plundered you will be plundered, and all who raided you will be raided." (Jeremiah 30:16) What they did comes back around to them. And that "nevertheless" is where the whole thing turns.

explanations.answer: They are made rulers over them
explanations.explanation: That would be a strange reward, friend, and it isn't in the verse. The LORD says, "all who devour you will be devoured, and all your adversaries—every one of them—will go off into exile." (Jeremiah 30:16) The ones who attacked don't get promoted. They get what they gave out.

Peace is not what's coming for them. The LORD says, "Those who plundered you will be plundered, and all who raided you will be raided." (Jeremiah 30:16) Their adversaries even "go off into exile." This is the turn, and it goes against the ones who attacked.
True, friend! The wound has no cure, and then comes the LORD: "I will restore your health and heal your wounds, declares the LORD." (Jeremiah 30:17) No cure, and He heals anyway. Don't miss that.

I see why you'd hesitate, since the LORD just said the pain has no cure (Jeremiah 30:15). But then He says, "I will restore your health and heal your wounds, declares the LORD." (Jeremiah 30:17) Both are in the passage. So this one is true.

explanations.answer: They call her an outcast no one cares for
explanations.explanation: That's the reason, baker. The LORD says, "I will restore your health and heal your wounds, declares the LORD, because they call you an outcast, Zion, for whom no one cares." (Jeremiah 30:17) Zion is Jerusalem. Others called her uncared for, and He steps in anyway.

explanations.answer: Her old allies finally asked Him to
explanations.explanation: Her allies aren't asking anybody for anything. The LORD already said, "All your lovers have forgotten you." (Jeremiah 30:14) His reason is that "they call you an outcast, Zion, for whom no one cares." (Jeremiah 30:17) The reason comes from Him, not from her friends.

explanations.answer: She healed her own wounds first
explanations.explanation: Not even close, friend. The LORD said her pain has no cure (Jeremiah 30:15). His reason for healing is "because they call you an outcast, Zion, for whom no one cares." (Jeremiah 30:17) She doesn't do the fixing. He does.

Not quite, friend. The LORD says, "the city will be rebuilt on her own ruins, and the palace will stand in its rightful place." (Jeremiah 30:18) Rebuilt is the word, and ruins are where it starts. So this one is false.

Yes, baker. The LORD says, "the city will be rebuilt on her own ruins, and the palace will stand in its rightful place." (Jeremiah 30:18) The ruins are the starting spot, and the palace goes right where it belongs. It's a rebuild.
That's the one! The LORD says, "Thanksgiving will proceed from them, a sound of celebration." (Jeremiah 30:19) Remember that cry of terror from earlier? Now it's a different sound coming out of them.

I get it, there was plenty of weeping before this. But the LORD says, "Thanksgiving will proceed from them, a sound of celebration." (Jeremiah 30:19) The sound changes. Thanksgiving is coming, and the weeping doesn't get the last word.

A warning is what you'd expect after the panic, friend. But the LORD says, "Thanksgiving will proceed from them, a sound of celebration." (Jeremiah 30:19) It's thanksgiving, not an alarm. The cry of panic from earlier turns into celebration.
Yes, friend! The LORD says, "Their leader will be one of their own, and their ruler will arise from their midst." (Jeremiah 30:21) He comes from their own people. Nobody has to bring in an outsider.

That's a long way from home, baker. The LORD says, "Their leader will be one of their own, and their ruler will arise from their midst." (Jeremiah 30:21) Their midst means right among them. Babylon isn't where he comes from.

Egypt's not in this verse, friend. The LORD says, "Their leader will be one of their own, and their ruler will arise from their midst." (Jeremiah 30:21) The leader rises up from the people themselves. He's one of their own.

That's it, baker. "Behold, the storm of the LORD has gone out with fury, a whirlwind swirling down upon the heads of the wicked." (Jeremiah 30:23) The whirlwind has a target, and the text names it. I'm still hanging onto my hat, though.

No, friend, the prophets aren't in the path of this one. The verse says the whirlwind comes "swirling down upon the heads of the wicked." (Jeremiah 30:23) The wicked are the ones named. Jeremiah can keep writing.

Good guess, since the exiles have been all over this passage. But the verse says the whirlwind comes "swirling down upon the heads of the wicked." (Jeremiah 30:23) The exiles are the ones the LORD is promising to restore. The storm is aimed at the wicked.

That's not how the verse goes, friend. The LORD's anger "will not turn back until He has fully accomplished the purposes of His heart." (Jeremiah 30:24) It stays until the job is done. So this one is false.

Right, baker. "The fierce anger of the LORD will not turn back until He has fully accomplished the purposes of His heart." (Jeremiah 30:24) It doesn't quit halfway. And the verse ends with this: "In the days to come you will understand this."
That's right, friend! The LORD says, "I will be the God of all the families of Israel, and they will be My people." (Jeremiah 31:1) Notice the word all. Every family is in.

I see why you'd say that, but the verse names a different group. The LORD says, "I will be the God of all the families of Israel, and they will be My people." (Jeremiah 31:1) It's the families of Israel He's talking about. The nations around them aren't named here.

Egypt didn't make the list this time, friend. The LORD says, "I will be the God of all the families of Israel, and they will be My people." (Jeremiah 31:1) It's the families of Israel, every one of them. The verse never mentions Egypt.
